claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy retains an fcc matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation of the alloy is governed by selective oxidation of Al and Cr.
Oxidizing conditions produce a continuous Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale.
The Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale formed under oxidizing conditions is protective and slow-growing.
Under reducing conditions, the initially formed oxide scale decomposes or loses adhesion.
Decomposition or loss of adhesion under reducing conditions causes localized scale spallation.
Scale failure under reducing conditions enhances internal oxidation.
Synergistic elemental effects cause Al and Cr to oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of Al and Cr forms a protective oxide layer in oxidizing environments.
Altered diffusion kinetics and gas-phase chemistry make the oxide scale less stable in reducing environments.
Scale decomposition and spallation accelerate degradation by permitting internal oxidation.
After oxidizing exposure, specimens will have a thin, continuous protective scale with only minor defects relative to the as-built baseline.
Under reducing exposure, an oxide will form early and then rapidly become discontinuous or spall.
Reducing exposure will cause deeper internal oxidation and faster degradation than oxidizing exposure.
The as-manufactured baseline has minimal oxidation or degradation before environmental exposure.
The proposed comparison is bounded to 800–900 °C and exposure durations of up to 100 hours.
Pure O2 represents the oxidizing condition, while N2 containing 5–10% H2 represents the reducing condition.
Microstructural inhomogeneities and local defect sites may influence oxidation independently of gas chemistry.
